segments.title: Why the 6-6 fleet still needed light forces
segments.body: The 6-6 plan aimed to make an attack on Japan costly enough to deter an invader. Six strong battleships formed its core, while six large armoured cruisers were expected to hold part of an enemy battle line until the battleships could win elsewhere. Japan paid for improvements to contemporary British battleship designs because it ordered only one or two ships at a time. Repeating the same extra cost across a British order of a dozen could substantially reduce the number affordable. Of each group of six, two ships would normally be fully operational and two more available to call upon, allowing four to be maintained for wartime operations close to Japan. Four battleships and four large armoured cruisers appeared at Tsushima. Destroyers brought a torpedo threat to this force that an invader also had to counter.

evidence.note: The 6-6 plan's battleship premiums, armoured-cruiser holding role, two operational plus two callable ships of each type, and accompanying destroyers and torpedoes.

segments.summary: Japan's 6-6 fleet plan paired its capital ships with destroyers, making a would-be invasion force confront more than the battle line.

segments.title: Japanese destroyer terms and Russia's torpedo-boat fears
segments.body: Kuchikukan is the Japanese term for destroyer, while gata marks a class designation. Urakaze is rendered as 'Sea Wind', with 'Bay Wind' offered as another possible translation. The preference for 'Sea Wind' combines its use in English-language sources with a personal preference for how it sounds as a destroyer name. Russian references to the Japanese torpedo boats they feared often concerned Japanese destroyers, so identifying the vessel type matters when reconstructing those light forces.

evidence.note: Kuchikukan and gata terminology, alternative Urakaze translations and the preference behind the chosen rendering, and Russian torpedo-boat references that often meant Japanese destroyers.

segments.summary: Japanese class terminology and Russian references to torpedo boats help distinguish the destroyers that formed part of Japan's feared light forces.

segments.title: What the captured Akatsuki reveals about Japanese doctrine
segments.body: The pictured Akatsuki was a captured Russian destroyer renamed after the original Japanese ship had been sunk by a Russian mine. Japan returned the prize to operations quickly and had little opportunity to adapt it during the war. Its use therefore reveals little about the development of Japanese destroyer design or doctrine. Captured French-built sailing ships in Royal Navy service provide the comparison: alterations made after capture offer evidence of the receiving navy's priorities, while the original foreign design reflects its original builder.

evidence.note: Akatsuki's replacement by a renamed Russian prize, its rapid return to operations, and the distinction between a captured design and adaptations made by its new navy.

segments.summary: Japan quickly returned a Russian prize to service as Akatsuki, leaving little opportunity for adaptations that could reveal Japanese design preferences.

segments.title: Light forces spread shipbuilding capacity across Japan
segments.body: Destroyers and torpedo boats gave Japan a practical way to distribute naval construction more widely than its larger warship programs. The navy expected exacting quality even as it spread orders among more builders. This work formed part of the second naval expansion bill, alongside smaller additions that adjusted larger plans when requirements changed. Light-force procurement helped build the industrial base used by later domestic destroyer classes.

evidence.note: Destroyer and torpedo-boat orders distributed construction and infrastructure across Japan under exacting quality standards, with smaller additions adjusting the second naval expansion program.

segments.summary: Destroyer and torpedo-boat orders spread construction work across Japanese yards while the navy continued to demand exacting standards.

segments.title: Perry's intervention and Japan's search for sea power
segments.body: Japan's naval expansion grew from its exposed coastline, weak internal communications, and dependence on sea routes. In the interpretation developed here, Commodore Matthew Perry's expedition appears as a minor episode in American narratives but as a lasting national trauma in Japan. The fear of being coerced, colonized, or stripped of cultural autonomy encouraged a strategy of becoming too difficult to attack. That fear encouraged the pursuit of an effective, balanced fleet. Mikasa was the centerpiece and status unit of the 6-6 structure, while Japan's weak internal communications made continued access to sea routes essential.

evidence.note: Japan's coastline and weak internal communications, the interpretation of Perry's intervention as a lasting national trauma, and the resulting emphasis on deterrence, maritime routes, and a balanced fleet.

segments.summary: Japan's forced opening and dependence on maritime communications provide the basis for an interpretation of its balanced fleet as a means of national survival.

segments.title: Perry's expedition and Japan's later strategic fears
segments.body: One proposed connection runs from Japan's forced opening to its later fears of losing its culture and being overwhelmed by others, including motives for entering the Second World War. In this critical reading, Perry completed his immediate mission, while his use of threats and rejection of accompanying diplomats undermined the basis for lasting relations. The American expectation that access to new trade, ships, and weapons would benefit Japan is set against the resentment generated by being compelled to accept them. Immediate mission success and the creation of a durable relationship are treated as different outcomes.

evidence.note: The proposed connection between Japan's forced opening and later strategic fears, criticism of Perry's preference for coercion without accompanying diplomats, and the distinction between mission success and lasting relations.

segments.summary: An interpretation of Perry's expedition connects Japan's forced opening with later strategic fears and distinguishes immediate mission success from lasting relations.

segments.title: Why destroyers began displacing torpedo boats
segments.body: Japan's first twelve destroyers came from Yarrow's Ikazuchi class and Thornycroft's Murakumo class, with construction spanning June 1897 to February 1900. Each carried a 12-pounder, five 6-pounders, and two 18-inch torpedo tubes. French torpedo-boat purchases reflected the influence of the Jeune Ecole, but enemy torpedo boats and British reliance on quick-firing guns exposed the limits of a force concentrated on torpedo attacks. Destroyers carried guns to fight enemy torpedo boats and destroyers alongside their own torpedoes. They initially operated with the torpedo boats while offering a route toward replacing them. For a few more crew members, Japan obtained a more versatile ship that suited its preference for vessels with greater individual capability.

evidence.note: The initial twelve destroyers' builders, June 1897 to February 1900 construction period and armament, French torpedo-boat influence, quick-firing guns, and the destroyer's broader fighting roles.

segments.summary: Japan's first twelve destroyers combined guns and torpedoes, giving them the flexibility to attack larger ships and defeat enemy light craft.

segments.title: Hayabusa torpedo boats as an industrial experiment
segments.body: Japan continued to buy first-class torpedo boats while its destroyer doctrine was taking shape. It bought Shirataka from Schichau in Germany, although the identification of the photograph shown in the video remains uncertain. Four Hayabusa-class boats came from Normand at Le Havre, six from the Kure Naval Arsenal, and five from Kawasaki. Learning from leading foreign builders and developing domestic production mattered more than standardization. The Hayabusa boats remained more torpedo-focused than the gun-and-torpedo destroyers, giving Japan a practical comparison between the two approaches. All fifteen Hayabusa-class boats were present at Tsushima, so the experiment also produced a substantial operational force.

evidence.note: Uncertainty over Shirataka's photograph, the four French-built and eleven Japanese-built Hayabusa boats, the priority given to acquiring capability over standardization, and all fifteen boats' presence at Tsushima.

segments.summary: Orders from Germany and France, followed by construction in Japanese yards, let Japan compare torpedo-boat technology while building its own industrial competence.

segments.title: Testing Thornycroft and Yarrow destroyer ideas
segments.body: Buying torpedo boats alongside destroyers kept both options open while Japan decided which type best suited its requirements. The larger Shirakumo and Akatsuki classes were initially ordered as strike leaders, with two ships from each of Thornycroft and Yarrow. They were roughly 50 tons heavier than their predecessors, with crews about twelve people larger and the familiar gun-and-torpedo fit retained. Thornycroft pursued extreme speed, while Yarrow emphasized manoeuvrability, so the orders compared two distinct design philosophies. The Thornycroft-built Shirakumo class exceeded its 30-knot requirement and approached 32 knots during exercises. Reports of the hulls beginning to plane capture the yard's aggressive pursuit of speed.

evidence.note: Parallel torpedo-boat and destroyer procurement, the strike-leader role, two ships from each British builder, increased displacement and crew, retained armament, reported planing, and exercise speeds near 32 knots.

segments.summary: The Shirakumo and Akatsuki orders let Japan compare two ambitious British design traditions and discover how much performance small destroyers could deliver.

segments.title: Destroyer speed becomes a tactical weapon
segments.body: The gap between a nearly 32-knot destroyer and an 18-knot battleship turned speed into operational freedom. Even a three-knot margin helps choose the timing of an engagement, while larger multiples increasingly control position, pace, and disengagement. A foreign fleet arriving off Japan could be slowed further by hull fouling after a long voyage, pushing the practical gap toward fifteen knots. At that point destroyers could move in and out of an enemy defensive envelope with considerable freedom. Japanese commanders could reinforce the armoured cruisers, help the battleships finish their engagement, or threaten a different target, forcing an attacker to bring a complete and balanced fleet. These early destroyers achieved that leverage while displacing no more than about 450 tons fully loaded.

evidence.note: Speed margins in three-knot increments, hull fouling after an overseas voyage, destroyers shifting between battleship and armoured-cruiser engagements, and displacement of about 450 tons or less.

segments.summary: A speed margin approaching fifteen knots over a travel-worn battle fleet gave Japanese destroyers freedom to choose their targets and reinforce either part of the 6-6 battle plan.

segments.title: Harusame exposes the trade-offs of domestic design
segments.body: The Harusame class was Japan's transition from importing examples to constructing complete destroyers at the Yokosuka and Kure naval arsenals. Its bow resembled Yarrow practice, other hull features reflected Thornycroft influence, and its rudder followed the Akatsuki class. Triple-expansion machinery and boilers drawn heavily from Yarrow patterns failed to deliver the hoped-for 30 knots, leaving the ships closer to 28 or 29 knots. The armament combined two versions of the 12-pounder, four 6-pounders, and two 18-inch torpedo tubes. The class nevertheless served in the Russo-Japanese War and took part at Tsushima.

evidence.note: Domestic construction at Yokosuka and Kure, combined foreign design influences, rudder and machinery, armament, speed shortfall, and Russo-Japanese War service.

segments.summary: Japan's first fully domestic destroyers blended lessons from imported designs, but their engines and boilers fell short of the hoped-for speed.

segments.title: Domestic destroyer production and the option of foreign advice
segments.body: Buying foreign destroyers gave Japan examples from which to learn construction methods and develop its own designs. Harusame combined a bow intended for manoeuvrability with a hull intended for speed, although the personal preference expressed here is to reverse that emphasis. A further possibility was to obtain foreign help with boilers and yard practice. Spain illustrates the contemporary option of having a foreign company establish a domestic yard, while Japan preferred to build its own industrial capability. Hiring a foreign builder to advise an existing naval arsenal is suggested as another possible arrangement. Its benefits remain a counterfactual judgment.

evidence.note: Domestic construction goals, a personal preference about bow and hull priorities, and possible foreign-owned yards or advisers as alternative routes to technical learning.

segments.summary: Harusame advanced Japan's goal of building its own destroyers, while leaving room to question whether foreign advisers could have eased its construction problems.

segments.title: War spreads destroyer production across Japan
segments.body: The Kamikaze-class design predated the Russo-Japanese War, but wartime urgency provided a strong case for expanding production. Only two ships had been commissioned by September 1905, so most of that expansion continued beyond the war that justified it. Japan divided 32 ships among eight naval and commercial yards. Yokosuka received the largest share, while Mitsubishi, Maizuru, Sasebo, Kawasaki, Kure, Osaka, and Uraga all contributed. Construction continued until June 1909, sustaining skills and defence investment after the fighting ended. Destroyer procurement expanded the fleet while spreading naval industry among more regions and builders.

evidence.note: Wartime justification for the Kamikaze program, only two ships commissioned by September 1905, and 32 vessels distributed across eight builders with construction continuing to June 1909.

segments.summary: The Russo-Japanese War accelerated a 32-ship Kamikaze program divided among eight yards, turning destroyer orders into years of industrial investment.

segments.title: Kamikaze-class lessons for night operations
segments.body: The Kamikaze class retained much of the Harusame hull, stack, and machinery arrangement, with its advances concentrated in operational refinement. Shorter funnels and spark or glow arresters addressed the risk that boiler emissions would reveal a destroyer at night. Japan's early concentration on destroyer night attacks may help explain why destroyers continued to lead its night operations into the Second World War. The contrasting British response after Jutland was to prepare the whole fleet to fight at night. Improved boilers could burn heavy fuel oil as well as coal, while short-barrelled 12-pounders replaced the earlier 6-pounders. Greater reliability and a stronger gun battery made the class a practical improvement.

evidence.note: Shortened stacks and spark suppression, the possible link between early Japanese destroyer night attacks and later doctrine, and Britain's whole-fleet night-fighting aim after Jutland.
Improved boilers, mixed coal-and-oil firing, 12-pounders replacing 6-pounders, and greater reliability.

segments.summary: Stack changes, spark suppression, improved boilers, and heavier light guns show Japan turning early destroyer experience into more reliable night-fighting ships.

segments.title: Destroyers protect the fighting edge at Tsushima
segments.body: At Tsushima, destroyers and torpedo boats supported the Japanese battleships and large armoured cruisers in several divisions. The First Squadron's supporting light forces included three destroyer divisions and the 14th Torpedo Boat Division. The Second Squadron had the Fourth and Fifth Destroyer Divisions alongside the Ninth and Nineteenth Torpedo Boat Divisions, while the Third Squadron's light forces were torpedo boats. Concentrating destroyers around the leading squadrons placed the more versatile craft beside the fleet's fighting edge. They could defeat enemy destroyers and torpedo boats, launch their own torpedo attacks, and in some cases carry mines. The Fourth Destroyer Division probably did more damage with mines than with torpedoes.

evidence.note: Destroyer and torpedo-boat allocations among the Japanese squadrons, their screening and attack roles, and the qualified comparison of Fourth Destroyer Division damage by mines and torpedoes.

segments.summary: Japan concentrated destroyer divisions around its leading squadrons, using them to screen the battle line, fight enemy light craft, launch torpedoes, and lay mines.

segments.title: Why Russia's Pacific reinforcements faced such poor odds
segments.body: Japan had 29 cruisers against Russia's nine and more torpedo boats than the Russian expedition had ships altogether. The comparison gives roughly 125 Japanese vessels against 38 Russian ships, although their individual capabilities varied. Several Russian heavy ships were poorly suited to a modern fleet action. Japan's ships mostly had clean hulls, recent maintenance, fresh supplies, and crews in good condition. Rozhestvensky had achieved an exceptional feat in bringing his expedition to battle, but the voyage left him facing decisive Japanese advantages in speed, numbers, and flexibility.

evidence.note: A recurring question about Russia's overseas deployment, comparative fleet strength, the unsuitability of coastal battleships for fleet action, and disparities in maintenance, supplies, and crew condition.

segments.summary: Russia sent an unbalanced expedition against a larger Japanese force fighting near its own bases, with coastal-defence ships assigned to unsuitable fleet duties.
segments.question: Why was sending Russia's Second and Third Pacific Squadrons around the world such a poor plan?
segments.answerShort: The Russian expedition lacked the supporting ships and local logistical advantages of Japan's balanced fleet. Its long voyage compounded those weaknesses, while coastal-defence battleships were poorly suited to the fleet action awaiting them.

segments.title: Alternative roles for Russia's coastal battleships
segments.body: Russia brought coastal battleships to a fleet action for which they were poorly suited. An alternative proposed here is to have sent them out before the war to reinforce the First Pacific Squadron's harbours and ports. They could also have extended protection while other ships raised speed for a breakout. That role might have required sacrificing the coastal ships so more capable vessels could escape. These are suggested uses for their limited capabilities, rather than events that took place at Tsushima.

evidence.note: Criticism of coastal battleships in modern fleet action and counterfactual alternatives: pre-war harbour reinforcement or possibly sacrificial breakout cover.

segments.summary: Russia's coastal battleships could have reinforced Far Eastern ports before the war and later covered a fleet breakout.

segments.title: Togo turns fleet depth into operational freedom
segments.body: Japan combined concentrated long-range gunfire with specialized light forces ready for skirmishing. Admiral Togo had many destroyers and torpedo boats available, with further supporting forces coming up. Their numbers let him risk losses in individual encounters while retaining the means to destroy the Russian fleet. This freedom did not mean that he wanted to sacrifice his ships. Defeating the expedition promised to settle the war at sea, giving him a reason to accept losses that achieved that larger result.

evidence.note: Concentrated Japanese gunnery, numerous skirmishing forces, and Togo's ability to accept light-force losses in order to defeat the Russian expedition.

segments.summary: Concentrated gunnery and abundant light forces let Admiral Togo control both the main action and its skirmishes while accepting risks Russia could not match.

segments.title: Why Tsushima and Trafalgar had different stakes
segments.body: A hypothetical Franco-Spanish victory at Trafalgar would still have left other British formations to fight, including the Western Squadron, Channel Fleet, and ships raised from reserve. Togo's force at Tsushima represented almost all immediately available Japanese naval power. There was no comparable Japanese force waiting behind it if Russia broke through. The Russian expedition was also its country's last practical attempt to reverse the war at sea. In this assessment, sending it was a decision driven by national pride despite the hopeless odds.

evidence.note: Hypothetical British formations remaining after a Franco-Spanish Trafalgar victory, Japan's concentration of available naval power, and the critical assessment of Russia's final expedition.

segments.summary: The Trafalgar comparison turns on the forces still available after a battle: Britain had other formations, while Japan had concentrated almost everything with Togo.

segments.title: Why improved Russian gunnery could not prevent disaster
segments.body: The loss figures given for Japan are 117 dead, 583 injured, and three torpedo boats sunk. Russian losses run to more than 5,000 dead, nearly 1,000 injured, and more than 6,000 prisoners, with every battleship either sunk or captured. Russia lost a vastly greater tonnage of shipping as well. The ships arrived in steaming order and struggled to establish a suitable battle formation. Their shooting nevertheless appears to have improved during the voyage, suggesting some success for Rozhestvensky's efforts to improve fire control and accuracy. Better gunnery alone could not overcome being outmanoeuvred.

evidence.note: Comparative deaths, injuries, prisoners and ship losses, the Russian formation problem, and the qualified judgment that gunnery improved during the voyage but could not overcome superior manoeuvre.

segments.summary: The scale of Russia's losses at Tsushima sits alongside a qualification: improved shooting could not compensate for the expedition's other disadvantages.

segments.title: Russian fear reveals the destroyers' deterrent effect
segments.body: Russian anxiety about Japanese torpedo craft during the voyage followed from knowledge of Japan's order of battle. The high command knew how numerous and capable those forces were and had reports of their fighting around Port Arthur. That knowledge helps explain the fear behind the Dogger Bank incident. Russia's expedition lacked enough supporting ships even by its own force-structure doctrine. Years of underinvestment had left too few assets available to send, while Japan could reinforce an engagement with more light forces.

evidence.note: Japanese reinforcement capacity, Russian knowledge of light-force operations around Port Arthur, Dogger Bank fears, and Russia's shortage of supporting assets.

segments.summary: Knowledge of Japan's numerous and combat-tested torpedo forces helps explain Russian fears during the voyage, while underinvestment left the expedition short of escorts.

segments.title: How Japan balanced its squadrons at Tsushima
segments.body: Japan's First Squadron combined four battleships with two armoured cruisers, four protected cruisers, thirteen destroyers, and four torpedo boats. The Second Squadron had six armoured cruisers and four protected cruisers, supported by eight destroyers and seven torpedo boats. Each formation combined heavy firepower with smaller vessels able to perform different tasks. Even the weaker Third Squadron was more balanced and organized than the Russian expedition. Nearby logistics and infrastructure helped Japan sustain this distribution of ships across its fleet.

evidence.note: First and Second Squadron ship-type counts, the Third Squadron comparison, and the value of nearby Japanese logistics.

segments.summary: The composition of Japan's First and Second Squadrons shows how cruisers and light forces supported the heavy ships within each formation.

segments.title: Umikaze tests the limits of turbine destroyers
segments.body: Inspired by Britain's pre-war Tribal class, Umikaze combined two 120 mm guns with oil-fired boilers, steam turbines, and a projected speed of 33 knots. Maizuru and Mitsubishi were being asked to build ships that pushed beyond their recent experience, making the class another deliberate technical experiment. Umikaze and Yamakaze were completed in 1911. Maintenance problems and very high fuel consumption led to mixed coal-and-oil firing and largely coastal patrol duties. The ships offered interesting exercise experience and later served as minelayers until 1936, but their performance did not justify ordering a large number.

evidence.note: Pre-World War I British Tribal inspiration and hull continuity with earlier Japanese destroyers.
Heavier guns, projected 33-knot turbine performance, builders and completion dates, fuel and maintenance problems, coastal patrols, and minelaying service through 1936.

segments.summary: The Umikaze class pursued faster, turbine-powered destroyers, but fuel use and maintenance problems showed the risks of adopting new machinery too quickly.

segments.title: Why an 80 mm Type 41 gun could still have a 76 mm bore
segments.body: The Type 41 light gun received a nominal 80 mm or 8 cm designation during Japan's move to metric terminology. Its origin lay in the British 12-pounder, and its bore apparently remained 76 mm. Whether the gun was bored out is disputed. Continued manufacture of ammunition to the 76 mm standard makes the reboring explanation seem unlikely.

evidence.note: Nominal 80 mm Type 41 designation, apparently unchanged 76 mm bore, acknowledged reboring claims, and ammunition dimensions offered against them.

segments.summary: Japan's metric gun names did not necessarily describe a changed bore: the Type 41 example turns on ammunition dimensions and a disputed reboring claim.

segments.title: Sakura restores range with proven machinery
segments.body: The Sakura class retreated from Umikaze's turbines to triple-expansion engines that Japanese yards could build confidently. It retained a 120 mm gun, the newer light gun, and two twin 18-inch torpedo launchers, preserving much of the desired combat improvement. Sakura and Tachibana were completed at Maizuru in 1912 and joined a force of more than fifty Japanese destroyers by the start of the First World War. Their machinery and fuel arrangements gave them better range than many close-coast predecessors, allowing deployments farther afield under the Anglo-Japanese Alliance. The class served until 1932 and established a practical operating standard, visible as well in the shift from four funnels to a three-funnel layout.

evidence.note: Return to triple-expansion engines, heavier guns and twin torpedo launchers, 1912 completion, long range and alliance deployments, service through 1932, and the three-funnel arrangement.

segments.summary: By returning to triple-expansion engines while retaining heavier guns and twin torpedo launchers, the Sakura class became a dependable long-range standard for wartime service.

segments.title: How Japan's Kawakaze became Italy's Audace
segments.body: Japan ordered the Urakaze pair from Yarrow before the First World War, but completion extended into wartime. Only one of the two ships went to Japan. The sister, originally named Kawakaze, was sold to Italy and became Audace. German forces later captured the ship in 1943 and used it during the Second World War.

evidence.note: Pre-war Yarrow order, wartime completions, Kawakaze's sale and renaming as Audace, and German capture in 1943. The stated Italian transfer date needs checking.

segments.summary: The two Yarrow-built ships ordered for Japan followed different careers: one reached Japan, while Kawakaze became Italy's Audace and later served under German control.

segments.title: Urakaze reopens the turbine and boiler experiment
segments.body: Japan returned to Yarrow for the Urakaze class to resume work on turbine propulsion and higher-pressure boilers. The ships exceeded 1,000 tons at full load, a considerable increase over Japan's first destroyers. The ship completed for Japan carried a 4.7-inch gun, three 12-pounders, and four 21-inch torpedo tubes in twin mounts. German diesel engines had been considered, but the First World War cut off that option and led to oil-fired Brown-Curtis turbines instead of Parsons machinery. Urakaze was consequently the first destroyer designed and built for Japan that relied entirely on oil and was not later converted to burn coal.

evidence.note: Yarrow boiler and turbine development, larger displacement and armament, the German diesel plan disrupted by war, and Urakaze's all-oil machinery. The horsepower figure is unclear.

segments.summary: The Yarrow-built Urakaze design gave Japan another route into high-pressure boilers, turbines, oil firing, and 21-inch torpedoes as war disrupted the original machinery plan.

segments.title: Kaba turns imported knowledge into warship exports
segments.body: The Kaba class continued Japan's earlier destroyer designs. The Japanese yards that built these ships later produced twelve related Arabe-class destroyers for France. The French regarded them as the most advanced destroyers in their inventory during the First World War. Japan had previously bought French torpedo boats to develop its own technology, so this sale reversed that earlier relationship. It may have been Japan's first sale of its own modern warship design abroad since Perry's intervention, although that priority claim has not been fully checked.

evidence.note: Kaba design continuity, twelve related ships built for France, the French assessment of their quality, and an explicitly unverified suggestion that this was Japan's first modern-warship export since Perry.

segments.summary: Japan's yards built twelve Arabe-class destroyers for France, reversing the earlier flow of torpedo-boat expertise from France to Japan.

segments.title: Japanese destroyers learn anti-submarine warfare at Malta
segments.body: The Kaba design used triple-expansion machinery driving three shafts, with a stated speed of 30 knots and a range of 1,600 nautical miles at 15 knots. Armament included a 4.7-inch gun and two twin 18-inch torpedo launchers. The same armament is tentatively identified on the ships built for France. Japanese ships of this class deployed with the cruiser Akashi to Malta to support Royal Navy anti-submarine operations in the Mediterranean. That service gave their crews practical experience of the anti-submarine capabilities needed during the war.

evidence.note: Triple-expansion machinery, speed and cruising range, gun and torpedo fit, qualified French-armament comparison, and Japanese anti-submarine operations from Malta with Akashi.

segments.summary: Kaba-class destroyers combined 30-knot speed and twin torpedo launchers with wartime service from Malta, gaining anti-submarine experience alongside Akashi.

segments.title: Why Japan's early destroyers vanished before the Second World War
segments.body: None of the earliest Japanese destroyer classes survived in Japanese service into the Second World War. Many ships built during the First World War also disappeared in the early and mid-1930s, whereas Britain and the United States retained comparable older vessels. Their retirement is questioned in light of Japan's fuel-supply difficulties: these ships burned coal and still offered possible secondary uses. Earlier anti-submarine experience suggests that they could have helped escort convoys. The argument concerns useful roles lost with the old hulls, without establishing why each class was discarded.

evidence.note: Japanese destroyer retirements in the 1930s compared with British and American retention, and the argument that coal-fired older ships could still have helped with convoy escort and anti-submarine work despite Japan's fuel problems.

segments.summary: Unlike many British and American contemporaries, most early Japanese destroyers were discarded in the 1930s despite their potential value for escort and anti-submarine duties.

segments.title: Why Tsushima's light forces faded from memory
segments.body: Tsushima is remembered chiefly as a victory for capital-ship gunnery. Japanese destroyers and torpedo boats represented a large share of pre-war investment and received several Russian battleships and coastal battleships as designated kills. A still larger torpedo tally might have driven greater international investment in destroyers and torpedoes before 1914. Public attention might also have remained fixed on expensive, high-status capital ships regardless of the result. Institutional prestige and the need to justify major programs can obscure the less glamorous ships that make a balanced fleet effective.

evidence.note: Light-force investment and credited kills at Tsushima, followed by an open counterfactual about torpedo victories, pre-1914 procurement, and the publicity given to capital ships.

segments.summary: Tsushima became famous as a long-range gunnery victory even though destroyers and torpedo boats shaped the battle and finished several Russian ships.
